history.hook_sig: i spent six hours chasing a ghost bug
texts: I spent six hours chasing a ghost bug where `WHERE status != 'cancelled'` silently dropped 40 percent of rows. The culprit was NULL hiding in plain sight.

NULL is not a value, it is the absence of one. Any comparison with NULL yields UNKNOWN, not TRUE or FALSE. So `status != 'cancelled'` evaluates to UNKNOWN for NULL rows and they vanish from the result set.
The fix is explicit: `WHERE status != 'cancelled' OR status IS NULL`. Or better, make the column `NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'` so the domain is closed and the optimizer can use indexes cleanly.

I now treat nullable boolean or status columns as a schema smell. If a column has three states, model it as an enum or a tinyint with a check constraint. NULL becomes a design decision, not an accident.

history.hook_sig: i spent four hours debugging why my customer
texts: I spent four hours debugging why my customer segmentation query returned zero rows. The logic was sound, indexes were perfect, explain analyze looked clean. Then I found it: a single NULL in the exclusion list turned my NOT IN into a black hole.

NOT IN with a subquery that returns NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row. Not false, UNKNOWN. And UNKNOWN rows get filtered out. This isn't a bug, it's three-valued logic working exactly as specified. Most of us learn NOT IN as "not in this list" and never read the fine print.

The fix is NOT EXISTS with a correlated subquery. It handles NULLs correctly because EXISTS only cares about row existence, not value comparison.

```sql
-- broken
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM excluded);

-- fixed
SELECT * FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM excluded e WHERE e.customer_id = c.id);
```

The excluded table had one row where customer_id was NULL from a bad import. That one NULL made NOT IN return UNKNOWN for all 2.3 million customers. NOT EXISTS ignored it and returned the correct 2.1 million. Same intent, radically different semantics.

texts: I spent three hours watching a healthy Postgres primary hit 100% CPU because one missing composite index turned a 5ms query into a sequential scan on 50 million rows. The query plan looked fine in staging. In production it melted the instance.

The concept is simple: Postgres chooses plans based on statistics, not data distribution. A query filtering on (tenant_id, status, created_at) with an index on (tenant_id, created_at) still scans every status value for that tenant. Statistics say "tenant_id is selective", they don't know status='pending' returns 90% of rows.

The fix was a single index: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ON events (tenant_id, status, created_at) WHERE status IN ('pending', 'processing'); Partial indexes shrink the B-tree by 80% and give the planner exact cardinality for the hot path. CPU dropped from 100% to 12% in minutes.

Most teams add more read replicas or increase instance size. The planner was begging for the right index shape all along. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on your slowest query, look for "Rows Removed by Filter" in the millions. That is your missing index.

texts: High connection pool wait time masquerades as database latency. The query runs in 2ms but sits in queue for 200ms. Scaling the database won't fix the queue.

Your application opens a pool of 20 connections. A slow downstream service holds each connection for 500ms. Requests pile up waiting for a free slot. Postgres CPU stays at 10 percent because the work never reaches it. The bottleneck is the pool, not the database.

I saw this on a checkout service. P99 API latency was 1.2s. Postgres p99 query time was 3ms. Pool wait time was 1.1s. Doubled the pool size from 20 to 40. P99 dropped to 15ms. No schema change, no index, no hardware upgrade. Just the pool.

Check pool wait time before you provision a larger instance. In Postgres use pg_stat_activity with state 'idle in transaction' and your client pool metrics. If wait time exceeds query time, the fix is in the pool config or the downstream call, not the database.

texts: A webhook consumer is not retry-safe just because its handler is idempotent. Record the event ID before side effects, or a retry can repeat the charge, email, or job.

history.hook_sig: retries do not make a write safe. without
texts: Retries do not make a write safe. Without an idempotency key and durable deduplication, a timeout can turn one payment request into two charges.

The client generates a unique key per user action and sends it with every retry. The server checks the key before executing. If a result exists, return it. If not, execute once, store the result keyed to the idempotency key, then return.

Store the idempotency key with the outcome, not the request body. A hash of the request changes when the client retries with a corrected payload. Key the result to the user action, not the bytes on the wire.

Keys need a TTL tied to the business window. A payment key lives for days. A like-button key lives for minutes. Clean up with a background job. Do not let the table grow unbounded or lookups will become the new bottleneck.

history.hook_sig: an idempotency key without a unique index is
texts: An idempotency key without a unique index is theater. The check-then-insert race window lasts microseconds but duplicates persist for years. A single unique constraint on the key column makes exactly-once semantics a database guarantee, not an application hope.

The race is simple: select where key exists, if not found insert. Two requests hit that gap simultaneously. Both see empty. Both insert. You now have two charges, two emails, two shipments. No application retry logic fixes this because the bug is the missing constraint.

Add a unique index on the idempotency key column. Insert with on conflict do nothing. The database serializes the winners. The second request gets a duplicate key error, treats it as success, and returns the existing row. Zero application coordination required.

The constraint also survives process crashes, network partitions, and deployed bugs that forget the check. If the column is a UUIDv7 or ULID, the index stays append-friendly. If it is a random UUID, accept the page splits or switch to a BIGINT sequence for the key.

texts: A payment service held a row lock on the orders table while calling a fraud-check API. The API averaged 800ms but occasionally spiked to 12s. During the spike 200 writers queued behind the single lock. P99 write latency jumped from 4ms to 9s.

history.hook_sig: a missing index on a foreign key column
texts: A missing index on a foreign key column locks the parent table during deletes. Postgres takes a ShareLock on the referenced table. Your unrelated inserts queue behind a single cascade.

Postgres checks referential integrity by scanning the child table. Without an index on the FK column that scan becomes sequential. The ShareLock blocks concurrent inserts on the parent. A single delete on a 10M-row child table can stall the parent for seconds.

I saw this on an orders table referencing users. The user_id column had no index. A cleanup job deleted 50K old orders. The users table froze for 12 seconds. New signups timed out. Adding the index dropped the lock time to 40ms.
The fix is one CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. No migration lock. No downtime. But most ORMs do not add FK indexes by default. Check pg_stat_user_indexes for seq scans on FK columns. That is your backlog.

texts: IF YOU WANT TO DESIGN CACHES THAT SURVIVE REAL TRAFFIC, STOP ASSUMING REQUESTS ARE EVENLY DISTRIBUTED. MEMORIZE THESE 5 HOT-KEY CHECKS:

Measure key-frequency distribution before you cache.

A single user id or product sku can absorb 80 percent of requests. Log the top-10 keys per minute and graph their share. If the head exceeds 30 percent, your cache tier is a hot-key amplifier, not a shield.

Protect the backend with local L2 and request coalescing.

A 10ms in-process TTL on the hottest key cuts origin load by orders of magnitude. Coalesce concurrent misses so only one request fetches while the rest wait. The pattern turns a thundering herd into a single round trip.

Size eviction windows to the skew, not the dataset.

LRU on a flat keyspace evicts the wrong data when one key dominates. Use segmented LRU or LFU with a tiny hot segment for the top 0.1 percent of keys. The cold segment absorbs churn without evicting the head.

texts: Reviewing every important change yourself makes you a team bottleneck. It centralizes context and delays feedback. The team ships at the speed of your review queue.

Designate code owners per subsystem.

A single owner reviews changes in their area within four hours. Others can approve but the owner merges. Context stays distributed. The queue never piles on one person.

Set a review SLA and automate reminders.

Flag PRs open longer than two hours. The author pings the owner in the team channel. If the owner is blocked, they delegate. Median review time drops from six hours to forty minutes.

Publish a lightweight review checklist.

Tests pass, migrations are backward compatible, logging covers the new path, no secrets in diff. Reviewers check the list, not every line. Consistency scales. Senior engineers stop re-explaining the same patterns.

history.hook_sig: i wrapped a payment confirmation in a transaction
texts: I wrapped a payment confirmation in a transaction that called a fraud-check API. The HTTP request took 12 seconds. During that hold the row lock on the orders table blocked every new checkout. Revenue dropped 18 percent in the hour before we killed the deploy.

The lock is not released until the transaction commits or rolls back. Postgres holds row-level locks for the full duration. An external call turns a millisecond critical section into seconds of serialization. No index or hardware fixes that.

We moved the fraud check before BEGIN. The service writes a pending order, calls the API, then opens a short transaction to flip the status. Lock hold dropped from 12 seconds to 3 milliseconds. Checkout p99 latency fell from 8.4 seconds to 42 milliseconds.
If the external service is down you still need idempotency and a retry queue. The pattern is: reserve locally, call out, confirm locally. Never let the database wait on the network.

texts:
IF YOU WANT TO EXPLAIN WHAT BREAKS AT 10X SCALE, STOP ADDING SERVERS TO EVERY BOX.

MEMORIZE THESE 5 SIGNALS:
Load balancer latency climbs first. When p99 of the LB itself rises, the backend is already saturated and queues are backing up upstream.
Database connection exhaustion. Not query slowness, just pool wait time. Check pg_stat_activity and pool wait stats before touching indexes.
Lock contention on a single hot row. Cache hit rate on the working set drops and threads start waiting on the same rows instead of doing work.
Cache hit ratio cratering under skewed access. Evenly distributed caches lie; real traffic hits a few keys and eviction kills throughput.
Replication lag on the primary. Write amplification shows up here before CPU or disk saturation, because the replica falls behind from sheer WAL volume.

texts:
IF YOU WANT TO FIX P99 LATENCY, STOP IGNORING CONNECTION POOL WAITS.

MEMORIZE THESE 5 MOVES:

Pool wait time masks as database slowness.

Postgres CPU sits at 15 percent while your API p99 climbs. The queue is the bottleneck, not the query.

Size the pool for concurrency, not cores.

A 32-core box with 100 active connections needs a pool of 50-80, not 32. Measure active sessions, not hardware.

Kill long-held connections before they starve the pool.

Set statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout. A single stuck request blocks every caller behind it.

history.hook_sig: switching a 50m row events table from uuidv4
texts: Switching a 50M row events table from UUIDv4 to UUIDv7 cut index size 35 percent and dropped p99 insert latency from 18ms to 4ms. UUIDv7 preserves insert locality like BIGINT but keeps global uniqueness. The sort order changed everything.

UUIDv4 writes land on random index pages. Every insert dirties a new page. The buffer pool churns. UUIDv7 embeds a timestamp prefix so new rows append to the right edge of the index. The working set stays small. Same global uniqueness, sequential writes.

The primary key index dropped from 22GB to 14GB. Buffer pool hit rate jumped from 87 percent to 96 percent. Write throughput doubled without adding hardware. The migration took one maintenance window with a concurrent index build and a brief rename swap.

UUIDv7 requires Postgres 17 or the uuid-ossp extension. If you are on an older version, ULID or a BIGINT identity column gives the same locality. The lesson is not the specific type. It is that insert order dictates index shape, and index shape dictates p99.

history.hook_sig: if you want to design reliable services, stop
texts:
IF YOU WANT TO DESIGN RELIABLE SERVICES, STOP TREATING RETRIES AS FREE.

MEMORIZE THESE 5 RETRY RULES:

Exponential backoff with jitter prevents thundering herds.

A fixed 100ms retry across 1000 clients creates a synchronized hammer. Add full jitter: sleep random(0, 2^attempt * base). The retry curve flattens and the downstream survives.

Idempotency keys turn retries from dangerous to safe.

Generate a UUIDv7 per client operation. Store the key with the result for 24 hours. Duplicate requests return the cached response. No double charges, no duplicate rows, no reconciliation jobs.

Retry budgets cap the blast radius.

Allow 10% of traffic to retry, not 100%. Track per-dependency budgets in a token bucket. When the bucket empties, fail fast. The caller sees a clean error instead of a cascading timeout.

history.hook_sig: uuidv7 fixes the write amplification of uuidv4 but
texts: UUIDv7 fixes the write amplification of UUIDv4 but keeps the 16-byte overhead. A BIGINT primary key still uses half the index space. Choose the key size your buffer pool can afford.
UUIDv7 embeds a timestamp so inserts land on the rightmost page. This eliminates the random I/O that makes UUIDv4 burn buffer pool. The index still stores 16 bytes per row versus 8 for BIGINT.

A 50 million row events table with UUIDv7 PK ran a 14 GB primary index. The same schema with BIGINT sat at 6.8 GB. Buffer pool hit rate moved from 91 percent to 97 percent. P99 insert latency dropped from 8 ms to 2 ms.
Use UUIDv7 when you need globally unique IDs without a coordination service. Use BIGINT when the table stays in one database and write throughput matters. The 8-byte savings compound at scale.

history.hook_sig: retrying a payment request without an idempotency key
texts: Retrying a payment request without an idempotency key can charge a customer twice. A timeout does not tell the client whether the first attempt committed.

The idempotency key is a client-generated token sent with every mutating request. The server stores the key with the response after the first successful execution. Any retry with the same key returns the stored response instead of re-executing the business logic.

Keys must be scoped to the business operation, not the HTTP request. Use a stable identifier like `order-12345-payment` rather than a random UUID per attempt. Store the key, response payload, and status code in a dedicated table with a unique index on the key and a TTL of 24 to 48 hours.

Common failure: generating a new key on every retry. The client must persist the key before the first send and reuse it on every retry. Another failure: releasing the key too early. Keep it until the payment reaches a terminal state so late retries after a network partition still deduplicate.

history.hook_sig: things that quietly break checkout after a payment
texts: THINGS THAT QUIETLY BREAK CHECKOUT AFTER A PAYMENT SUCCEEDS:

Payment captured but order creation fails.

A network blip, a deadlock, or a validation error rolls back the order transaction. The payment gateway already moved money. You now have revenue with no order record, no fulfillment trigger, and a reconciliation nightmare that manual ops must untangle.

Idempotency key missing or reused across retries.

The client retries the checkout call with a new key. The payment service treats it as a fresh capture. The order service sees a duplicate key and rejects it. One charge succeeds, the other returns 409. The customer sees two charges, support sees one order, finance sees a mismatch.

Webhook arrives before the order service is ready.

Payment gateway posts "captured" to your webhook endpoint. The order service is still booting, deploying, or rate-limited. The webhook times out or gets a 5xx. The gateway retries hours later. By then the idempotency window expired. The payment is captured, the order never created, and the retry creates a duplicate charge.

history.hook_sig: if you want to keep a cache from
texts: IF YOU WANT TO KEEP A CACHE FROM TAKING DOWN YOUR DATABASE, STOP TREATING TTL AS A LOAD-SHEDDING PLAN. MEMORIZE THESE 5 MOVES:

Stagger TTLs with jitter so hot keys never expire in sync.

A fixed 300-second TTL on a key hit 50K times per minute creates a synchronized stampede when it expires. Add random jitter of 0-60 seconds per key instance. The rebuild load spreads across a minute instead of hitting the database in a single thundering herd.

Refresh hot keys probabilistically before TTL expires.

Track request rate per key. When a key exceeds 100 requests per second, start an async rebuild at 80 percent of its remaining TTL. The background worker fetches fresh data while the stale value serves traffic. Rebuild latency drops from p99 to near zero, and the database never sees the spike.

Coalesce concurrent misses with a single-flight lock.

First cache miss acquires a distributed lock (Redis SETNX with 5-second TTL). That request rebuilds the value. All other waiters block on the lock and read the fresh entry when it lands. Ten thousand concurrent requests for the same key become one database call. For ultra-hot keys, add a 100-millisecond local in-memory cache to absorb the tail.

history.hook_sig: things that quietly break read-after-write consistency:
texts: THINGS THAT QUIETLY BREAK READ-AFTER-WRITE CONSISTENCY:

Async replicas with stale reads
Your write hits the primary. The read goes to a replica lagging 200ms. The user sees old data. Fix: route read-your-writes to the primary or wait for replication catch-up.

Missing causal consistency tokens
Service A writes. Service B reads without the version token. The load balancer sends B to a stale replica. Fix: pass the write LSN or timestamp and require the replica to reach it.

Silent failover during lag
Primary fails. Replica promotes with 50ms unreplicated writes. Clients read the new primary and miss those writes. Fix: synchronous commit for critical paths or application-level conflict resolution.

history.hook_sig: if you want your queues to drain under
texts:
IF YOU WANT YOUR QUEUES TO DRAIN UNDER LOAD, STOP IGNORING BACKPRESSURE SIGNALS.

MEMORIZE THESE 5 CONTROL MOVES:

Set a hard max queue depth and reject new work at the edge.

A bounded queue turns unbounded latency into explicit 429s. The client can retry with backoff. An unbounded queue turns a spike into an OOM kill that takes the whole node down.

Scale consumers by observed drain rate, not by queue length.

Queue length is a lagging indicator. Drain rate (messages/sec processed) tells you if you are catching up. Add consumers only when drain rate exceeds arrival rate for a sustained window, otherwise you just add more contention.

Shed load before the database feels the spike.

A circuit breaker that trips on p99 latency or error rate protects the downstream store. Returning a degraded response (stale cache, empty list) is better than letting the retry storm amplify the outage. The queue is a shock absorber, not a storage tank.

history.hook_sig: if you want to design multi-region systems, stop
texts:
IF YOU WANT TO DESIGN MULTI-REGION SYSTEMS, STOP ASSUMING FAILOVER IS INSTANT.

MEMORIZE THESE 5 TRADEOFFS:

Synchronous replication caps write latency at the speed of light between regions.

A 50ms round trip means every commit waits 50ms. At 10K writes per second that is 500 seconds of cumulative stall per second. Async replication removes the wait but introduces a replication lag window where failover loses data.

DNS-based failover relies on TTL expiration and client resolver caches.

A 60-second TTL with sticky resolvers can leave 30 percent of traffic hitting the dead region for five minutes. Health-check-driven load balancers cut this to seconds but add a control-plane dependency that itself must be multi-region.

Stateful services need a split-brain policy before the partition happens.

Quorum requires a majority of nodes. In a two-region deployment that means one region is primary and the other cannot promote alone. Three regions solve quorum but triple the replication cost and operational surface.
